intro: Every match needs a start. In judo, players bow. In boxing, a bell rings. In school wrestling, two wrestlers shake hands and a whistle blows. In fencing, the referee calls out in French.
Matches also need rules. Rules say who meets whom. They say what gear to wear. In this unit, you will meet boxing gloves, fencing masks, weight classes and the groups that write rule books.
By the end, you can name how a room starts a match. You can tell one rule that keeps players safe. You can tell when girls and women got their own matches.
bigQuestion: How do signals and rules make a match fair and safe?

write.prompt: Pick one sport from this unit. Tell or draw how a match starts. Then tell one rule that keeps players safe or fair. Name the rule book or group and the year.
tips: Use a word from the unit, like bow, bell or salute.
Name the rule book or group, like the Queensberry Rules.
Tell the year the rule or group began.

title: Fair Start

chapters.title: Bow, Handshake, Whistle
chapters.bigQuestion: How do different rooms show that a fair match has begun?

story.title: Two Rooms, One Minute
story.kicker: At nine o'clock, two classes start in two different ways.
paragraphs: It is nine o'clock at a school in Illinois. In the big gym, a PE teacher lifts a silver whistle. She blows it once. Thirty children stop and turn to face her.
Down the hall is a small room with a soft mat. A judo club meets there. The students stand in a line. They bow to the teacher, and the teacher bows back.
Nobody in either room says, "We are starting now." Still, everyone knows. In one room, the sign is a sound. In the other room, the sign is a bow.

Rooms all over the world have signs like these. A bell rings in boxing. Fencers raise their blades to each other. Wrestlers shake hands. Each sign says the same thing: the match is fair, and it starts now.
story.think: What sign tells your class that it is time to begin?

lessons.title: The Bow in Judo
lessons.mainIdea: In judo, players bow at the start and the end of a match.
reading: Judo began in Tokyo, Japan, in 1882. Its first school was the Kodokan. Its founder was Kanō Jigorō. In judo, the bow is called *rei*. Players bow before a match. They bow again after it ends.
In Japan, a bow is an everyday greeting. People bow to say hello and thank you. In judo, a bow means respect for the other player. After the bow, the referee says *hajime*. That word means "begin."

words.d: the Japanese word for a bow; judo players bow at the start and end of a match
a Japanese word that means begin; the judo referee says it to start a match

look.title: Two White Jackets
look.text: Look at two players in white jackets. They stand on a square mat, facing each other. Both bend forward a little at the waist. A referee waits at the side. Nobody has moved toward the other yet.
look.prompt: Is this match starting or ending? What clue helps you tell?

lessons.title: The Dojo Room
lessons.mainIdea: Many students bow when they walk into a dojo and when they leave it.
reading: A *dojo* is a room for a Japanese art. Judo and karate use dojos. The word means "place of the way." In many dojos, students bow at the door. They bow when they come in and when they go out.
The bow is a greeting and a thank-you. It is not a prayer. People of many religions study judo and karate. Some have no religion at all. Each dojo sets its own customs.

words.d: a room for studying a Japanese art such as judo or karate; the word means place of the way

lessons.title: The Boxing Bell
lessons.mainIdea: In boxing, a bell starts and ends each round.
reading: A boxing match is cut into parts called *rounds*. In 1867, the Queensberry Rules set each round at three minutes. They set a one-minute rest between rounds. Many boxing matches still use these times.
A *bell* rings to start each round. It rings again to end it. The referee calls the two boxers to the middle first. Often the boxers touch gloves. That is a way to say, "Let's have a fair match."

words.d: one part of a boxing match; the Queensberry Rules made each round three minutes
the sound that starts and ends each round in boxing

check.q: What do boxers often do before a match?
check.why: Boxers often touch gloves at the start. It says, let's have a fair match.

lessons.title: A Handshake and a Whistle
lessons.mainIdea: In school wrestling, wrestlers shake hands, and a referee's whistle starts the match.
reading: School wrestling in the United States starts with a handshake. The two wrestlers shake hands first. The *referee* blows a whistle to start. A match has three periods of two minutes each.
At the end, the wrestlers shake hands again. Then the referee raises the winner's hand. In Illinois, the IHSA runs school wrestling. The IHSA began in 1900.

words.d: the person who runs a match and makes sure the rules are kept
a greeting where two people hold hands for a moment; wrestlers shake hands before and after a match

lessons.title: Salt in the Sumo Ring
lessons.mainIdea: Before a sumo bout, wrestlers toss salt into the ring to make it clean.
reading: Sumo comes from Japan. Before a bout, many wrestlers toss a handful of *salt* into the ring. The custom comes from *Shinto*. Shinto is an old religion of Japan. In Shinto, salt stands for making a place clean.

A referee called the *gyoji* stands in the ring. He wears bright silk robes. He holds a wooden fan. The two wrestlers start at the same moment, when both are ready. The gyoji points his fan at the winner.

words.d: an old religion of Japan; the salt custom in sumo comes from it
the referee in sumo; he wears silk robes and holds a wooden fan

lessons.title: The Fencer's Salute
lessons.mainIdea: Fencers salute each other before a bout and shake hands after it.
reading: In fencing, a bout starts with a *salute*. Each fencer raises the blade toward the other. They salute the referee too. The world rules for fencing ask for this salute.

Then the referee speaks *French*. The world fencing group began in Paris. First comes "En garde." Next comes "Prêts?" That means "Ready?" Then comes "Allez!" That means "Go!" After the bout, the fencers shake hands.

words.d: a sign of respect; fencers raise their blades to each other before a bout
the language of France; fencing referees use French words to start a bout

chapters.title: Rules That Keep Players Safe
chapters.bigQuestion: How did new rules and new gear make matches safer and fairer?

story.title: The Old Book of Rules
story.kicker: A class opens a history book and finds gloves, masks and mats.
paragraphs: A second-grade teacher sets a big history book on the rug. The cover is green and worn. She opens it to a page with an old drawing. Two men box with bare hands.
"Long ago, boxers wore no gloves," she says. She turns the page. Now there is a pair of puffy leather gloves. "In 1867, a new set of rules asked for these."
She turns more pages. There is a fencing mask made of wire. There is a thick mat for wrestling. There is a list of weights, from light to heavy.
"Each of these came from a rule," she says. "People wrote rules to keep players safe. They wrote rules to make matches fair." A student points at the mask. "When did they start using that?"
story.think: What is one rule at school that keeps you safe?

lessons.title: From Bare Hands to Gloves
lessons.mainIdea: Boxers once fought with bare hands, and later rules asked for gloves.
reading: Jack Broughton was a boxer in London. In 1743, he wrote boxing *rules*. One rule kept a fallen boxer safe. He could not be hit while down. Broughton also used padded *gloves* for practice. In real matches, boxers still used bare hands.

In 1867, the Queensberry Rules asked for gloves in matches. The change took time. In 1892, John L. Sullivan and James J. Corbett boxed with gloves in New Orleans. It was a famous title match under the new rules.

words.d: padded coverings for the hands; boxing rules from 1867 asked boxers to wear them
written directions everyone in a sport agrees to follow

look.title: Broughton's Rule
look.text: A boxer who is down on his knees may not be hit while he is down.
look.prompt: How did this rule help keep a boxer safe?

check.why: Jack Broughton wrote a set of boxing rules in London in 1743.

check.q: Which rules asked boxers to wear gloves in matches?

check.q: What did Broughton's rule say about a boxer who was down?

check.why: Broughton's rule said a boxer who was down could not be hit.

lessons.title: The Fencing Mask
lessons.mainIdea: Fencers wear a wire mask, and today their touches are counted by electric lights.
reading: Fencers wear a *mask* made of strong wire mesh. It covers the whole face. Masks like this came into use in the 1700s. Before that, fencing practice was much less safe.

Long ago, people watched closely to see each touch. Now a wire runs from each fencer to a box. A light turns on when a blade tip lands. This is *electric scoring*. It came to the Olympics one sword at a time.

words.d: a wire mesh cover that keeps a fencer's face safe
a system of wires and lights that shows when a fencer's blade lands a touch

lessons.title: Groups by Weight
lessons.mainIdea: Weight classes let players meet others close to their own size.
reading: In many combat sports, players are put in groups by how much they weigh. These groups are called *weight classes*. A light player meets another light player. A heavy player meets a heavy player.
Judo came to the Olympics in Tokyo in 1964. It had four groups. Three were weight classes. The fourth was an open group for any weight. Anton Geesink of the Netherlands won the open group.

words.d: a group of players who weigh about the same; they compete against each other

lessons.title: Groups That Write the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: World groups write the rule books that referees follow.
reading: Who writes the rules for a sport? Often it is a world group called a *federation*. Many countries belong to it. They agree on one rule book. Then a match in Paris and a match in Chicago use the same rules.

The International Fencing Federation began in Paris in 1913. The International Judo Federation began in 1951. World Taekwondo began in Seoul, South Korea, in 1973. Each one trains referees to use its rules.

words.d: a group of many countries that agree on one set of rules for a sport

lessons.title: Headgear in School Wrestling
lessons.mainIdea: School wrestlers in the United States must wear headgear that covers their ears.
reading: Most U.S. high schools use wrestling rules from the *NFHS*. That stands for the National Federation of State High School Associations. It began in 1920. Its rules say every wrestler must wear *headgear*.

Headgear is a set of hard cups and straps. It covers the ears. It helps keep ears from getting hurt. School wrestling also happens on a thick, padded mat. Olympic wrestlers may choose whether to wear headgear.

words.d: the National Federation of State High School Associations; it writes rules for many U.S. school sports
hard cups and straps that cover a wrestler's ears

lessons.title: Doors That Opened
lessons.mainIdea: Over time, rules changed so that girls and women got their own matches.
reading: For a long time, many matches were only for men. Women first fenced at the Olympics in 1924, in Paris. Women's judo joined the Olympics in 1992, in Barcelona, Spain.

In Illinois, girls wrestled on school teams for many years. Most often they wrestled against boys. Then the IHSA made a girls *state final*. The first one was held in 2022. Now girls have their own state champions.

words.d: the last and biggest meet of the school year, where state champions are named
